definition_en: The written supreme law of the United States, adopted in 1787. It sets up the government, defines its powers and protects the rights of the people.
A change or addition to the Constitution. Proposed by two-thirds of Congress and ratified by three-quarters of the states; there are 27.
The first ten amendments to the Constitution, ratified in 1791, protecting basic rights such as freedom of speech, religion and the press.
The document adopted on July 4, 1776, announcing that the colonies were free from Britain and that all people are created equal.
A form of government in which the people hold power and exercise it through elected representatives under law.
The principle that everyone — citizens, leaders and the government — must follow the law; no one is above it.
The idea that the government’s power comes from the people: the meaning of “We the People.”
The U.S. economic system: a free-market economy in which individuals and businesses own property and decide what to make, buy and sell.
Eighty-five essays by Madison, Hamilton and Jay, written as Publius, explaining and supporting the Constitution.
Dividing government among the legislative, executive and judicial branches so that no one branch becomes too powerful.
The powers each branch has to limit the others — a veto, an override, judicial review, Senate confirmation.
The legislative branch: the Senate (100 members) and the House of Representatives (435 voting members). It writes federal laws.
The chamber of Congress with two members from every state, each serving a six-year term.
The chamber of Congress with 435 voting members divided among the states by population, each serving two years.
The President’s power to refuse to sign a bill. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.
The Vice President and the heads of the executive departments, who advise the President.
The body of electors, chosen state by state, that formally elects the President and Vice President.
The highest court in the United States, with nine justices who serve for life.
The sharing of power between the national government and the states; the 10th Amendment leaves the states every power not given to the federal government.
The President’s role as head of the armed forces.
The legal process by which a person born outside the United States becomes a citizen.
The promise new citizens make: to give up other loyalties, defend the Constitution, obey the laws and serve the nation if needed.
A short promise of loyalty to the flag and to the United States.
The system under which men aged 18 through 25 register so a military draft could be held fairly if ever needed.
A fee once charged to vote, banned by the 24th Amendment in 1964.
A group of citizens who decide the facts in a trial. Serving on one is a duty only citizens have.
A territory settled and ruled by a distant country; the thirteen American colonies were ruled by Britain.
The colonists’ complaint that Britain taxed them while giving them no seats in Parliament.
The 1787 meeting in Philadelphia where the Founding Fathers wrote the Constitution.
The first, weak national government of the United States, replaced by the Constitution in 1789.
Lincoln’s 1863 order freeing the slaves in the Confederate states.
The years after the Civil War when the South was rebuilt and the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments were adopted.
The United States, and in the Civil War the Northern states that stayed loyal to it.
The eleven Southern states that left the Union in 1861 and fought the Civil War.
The rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union from the late 1940s to 1991, fought through alliances and proxy wars rather than directly.
A political and economic system in which the state owns property and controls the economy; stopping its spread was the main U.S. concern of the Cold War.
The 1950s–60s movement, led by Martin Luther King, Jr., that fought to end racial discrimination.
The longest economic recession in modern history, beginning with the stock market crash of 1929.
Land under U.S. sovereignty that is not a state, such as Puerto Rico or Guam.
Latin for “Out of many, one”: the nation’s first motto.
The country’s official song, “The Star-Spangled Banner.”
One of the eleven days set by law on which federal offices close, such as Independence Day and Thanksgiving.
